v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season10-bible-v1.0.1.md row a10e05, writer brief a10e05-v1.0.0.md, LATENT catalog v1.0.77 and latent-syllabus-v1.0.3.md. a10e04's next field was honoured: a concrete plant's night pours, and storing a model's weights in fewer bits in plain words: 16-bit, 8-bit and 4-bit copies, and measuring what each one loses. Keeps apart from a8e02 (there 4-bit weights train an add-on cheaply; here a squeezed model is served and what it lost is measured), from a1e08 (there a model size is chosen; here the same model is stored smaller), from s3e13 (concrete is only the product: no old house, no foundations) and from a10e01's furnace (a ready-mix plant has no kiln, oven or furnace). The title's miniature is only a metaphor for a model made smaller; no village appears. Shared given data: Llama 3.1 70B, 70.6 billion weights, 80 layers, 8 key/value heads of 128 numbers; 141 billion bytes in 16-bit (about 132 GB on the meter); FP8 about 66 GB; 4-bit (AWQ) about 33 GB plus about 1 GB of scales (one 16-bit scale per group of 128 weights); working memory 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 327,680 bytes = 320 KB a token; H100 80GB, 3.35 TB/s, 4 GB of working space a card; sizes in the meter's units (1 GB = 1,024 MB), speeds in the maker's. The plant's own figures, never a source's: English set (200 procedure questions) 16-bit 188, FP8 188, 4-bit 186; numbers set (160 past tickets with checked figures, built in April) 16-bit 154, FP8 153, 4-bit 136; reply 1's 400 questions 376 and 372; reply 3's self-check 139 of 160 (the second try agreed with 21 of the 24 wrong totals); night peak 6 chats, the cold case's 24; a chat counted at 1,600 tokens. Arithmetic (all in sims/a10e05-v1.0.0.js): 38 x £115 = £4,370.00, printed £437.00 (£11.50 a cubic metre); 12 x £106 = £1,272.00, printed £1,212.00; 6 x £98 = £588.00, printed £558.00; 154 - 136 = 18 more wrong in 160, 11% (11.25); wrong tickets in a night of 22: 16-bit 0.8, FP8 1.0, 4-bit 3.3, self-check 2.9; FP8 on one card 80 - 66 - 4 = 10 GB, 32,768 tokens, 20 chats against a peak of 6; 16-bit on two cards 20 GB, 65,536 tokens, 40 chats; 4-bit on one card 42 GB, 137,625 tokens, 86 chats; FP8 on two cards 86 GB, 281,804 tokens, 176 chats; $3.99 x 730 = $2,913 a month a card, two $5,825, the gap $2,912; fastest writing at 3.35 TB/s about 47 tokens a second for FP8 on one card (and for 16-bit on two, before the cards' swaps), about 92 for the 4-bit copy. Timeline: launch in March 2026 on two cards in 16-bit; the numbers set built and run on 16-bit in April; Thursday 17 September 2026 at 17:30 the 4-bit copy signed off on the English set (186 against 188); 18:00 the switch to one card; 22 tickets from 18:00 to 23:40, numbers 481 to 502; 19:05 ticket 484 and 21:30 ticket 493 wrong and signed on site; 23:40 ticket 502 prints in the batching cabin (the alert); 23:45 the operator stops the assistant writing totals, checks all 22 by hand and works out every total by hand until 06:00; the post at about 06:30 on Friday 18 September; the 4-bit copy still live, the next tickets from 18:00 that day. Cold case: 3 months later, 18 September to Friday 18 December 2026 (FP8 from Friday 18 September; a second night crew from Monday 7 December; the peak of 24 on Thursday 10 December). Card prices stated as close to one provider's dollar list price (Lambda, $3.99 to $4.29 a card hour, read 16 October 2026). Legal: the plant is in England; a wrong ticket is stated conditionally under the plant's terms of sale, not legal advice. Standards notes conditional. Sources read 16 October 2026.
title: The Miniature Village

post.author: u/batch_cabin_aslaug
post.title: I run the night batching at a concrete plant. At 23:40 our assistant printed a ticket for 38 m³ at £115 a cubic metre: total £437.00. In perfect English.

blocks.text: I'm Aslaug, night batching operator at Eskmere Concrete, a ready-mix plant in England. We mix concrete for night pours and send it out in drum trucks. A batching computer weighs each load from its own recipes; the assistant only does paperwork.

The assistant is a language model, a program that writes text in small pieces called tokens. From each order's mix, volume and price per cubic metre it writes the delivery ticket and the order summary. Crews also ask it questions in chats, 6 at most.
It's Llama 3.1 70B: 70.6 billion weights, the learned numbers a model is made of. Since launch in March each has been stored in 16 bits, a bit being one 0 or 1.
Eight bits make a byte: 141 billion bytes, about 132 GB, a GB being about a billion bytes.

That's too big for one graphics card, a card for short (case a10e01): an NVIDIA H100 holds 80 GB and keeps 4 GB as working space. So ours ran on two, at $3.99 each an hour, close to one provider's dollar list price: $5,825 a month.
Each token of a chat also keeps 320 KB (327,680 bytes) of working memory on the card (case a10e03).

No change goes live until it passes a task set: one kind of job, with right answers agreed in advance. Our sign-off set: 200 English questions about our procedures. Signing off: run the set on each copy, count right answers, compare.

In April the office built a second task set, the numbers set: 160 past tickets with checked figures. The 16-bit model got 154: a slip in one ticket of 27, which the office's morning check, every ticket against its order, catches. The sign-off stayed English.

At 18:00 on Thursday 17 September, IT switched to a smaller copy of the same model, to halve the bill. Eyvind, our IT lead, calls it a map redrawn at a smaller scale: the roads stay, the footpaths blur.

Squeezing takes two steps. First, the weights are split into groups of 128, each with a scale: a ruler sized to its largest weight. Then each weight is rounded to the nearest of 16 marks on that ruler; 16 bits allowed 65,536 values. That's 4 bits a weight: about 33 GB plus 1 GB of scales, one card, $2,913 a month.

blocks.title: SIGN-OFF · smaller copy, 4 bits a weight, one card
items: Switch at 18:00 tonight. Saves $2,912 a month.

blocks.text: Each line shows the time, the ticket, the order, the total the assistant worked out (a sum: volume times price) and my sum by hand.

19:05  ticket 484  12 m³ × £106         printed £1,212.00  by hand £1,272.00
21:30  ticket 493   6 m³ × £98          printed £558.00    by hand £588.00
23:40  ticket 502  38 m³ C32/40 × £115  printed £437.00    by hand £4,370.00
£11.50 a cubic metre. Less than the sand in it.

Ticket 502 printed in my cabin as the first truck loaded. At 23:45 I checked all 22 tickets by hand: three wrong. 484 and 493 had gone out, signed on site. Eyvind, on the phone, said it passed the sign-off, so I worked out every total by hand until 06:00.

Top row, as printed: ticket 484 at 19:05, 12 cubic metres at £106, printed £1,212.00; ticket 493 at 21:30, 6 cubic metres at £98, printed £558.00; ticket 502 at 23:40, 38 cubic metres at £115, printed £437.00. Bottom row, by hand: £1,272.00, signed on site; £588.00, signed on site; £4,370.00, held in the cabin. The other 19 tickets matched.

blocks.text: By hand: 38 × £115 = £4,370.00. Three wrong in 22; under 16 bits, a slip about once a night. The 4-bit copy is still live; tonight's tickets start at 18:00. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that cabin is haunted, though a ticket in perfect English for a tenth of the price is a cold thing to hand a driver. What Eyvind did has a name: quantization, storing each weight in fewer bits, the map redrawn smaller. Your launch copy's 16 bits are FP16, short for 16-bit floating point: each weight kept as a few digits plus a point that can move, so tiny and large weights both keep their detail. Two questions. On ticket 502, which figures did the assistant copy from the order, and which did it work out? And has the 4-bit copy ever been scored on the numbers set?

replies.author: u/batch_cabin_aslaug
replies.text: Copied, and right: 38 m³, C32/40, £115. Worked out, and wrong: the total. The same on 484 and 493. And no. The numbers set has only ever been run on the 16-bit model, in April.

replies.author: u/gradient_ghost
replies.text: One more pair of names, since they come up in every list of copies. Eight bits come in two forms: FP8, short for 8-bit floating point, and INT8, short for 8-bit integers, whole numbers with a scale for each group, as your copy does at 4 bits.

comments.author: u/one_percent_eyvind
comments.text: IT lead. I signed it off, and I'd sign it again. My copy is INT4, short for 4-bit integers, made with AWQ, activation-aware weight quantization, which protects the weights that matter most before rounding. It's the usual way to fit a 70B model on one card. 186 against 188 is one percent; one bad ticket is bad luck, not the model. The numbers set is 160 old tickets the office typed up in April; I wouldn't hang a switch on it. If you want more certainty, make the sign-off set bigger: 200 more English questions, then run, count, compare again. Half the bill is $2,912 a month.

replies.author: u/batch_cabin_aslaug
replies.text: It was three tickets, not one.

replies.author: u/one_percent_eyvind
replies.text: Three of 22 on a first night. The English set is how we've always signed off, and it passed.

comments.author: u/morning_office_obiageli
comments.text: Office. My morning check compares every ticket with its order before we invoice, so Thursday's three get corrected before any bill goes out. But 484 and 493 were signed on site. If the ticket is our bill to the customer, a wrong price may matter under our terms of sale; I'm asking our solicitor, and nothing here is legal advice. My fix keeps the cheap copy: have it check its own sums. It writes the ticket, works the total out a second time, compares the two, and prints only if they agree. Two tries catch a slip.

comments.author: u/two_cards_thokozani
comments.text: Plant manager. Put it back the way it ran from March to Thursday and leave it there. Two cards and 16 bits gave us a slip about once a night, and the morning check caught every one. The extra $2,912 a month is less than the £3,933 that ticket 502 was short. I'd rather pay for a card than explain a price to a customer.

reply.prompt: It's 06:30 on Friday 18 September. The 4-bit copy is still live, and tonight's tickets start at 18:00. What should the plant change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Score each smaller copy on every task set, sums included, then switch.
options.part2: By 15:00 on Friday Eyvind had made a third copy, FP8, about 66 GB, and run both task sets on all three: run, count, compare. English: 16-bit 188, FP8 188, 4-bit 186. Numbers: 154, 153 and 136. Only FP8 stayed within 1% on both; the 4-bit copy had lost 18 tickets in 160, 11%, in line with Thursday's three wrong in 22. FP8 fits one card with 80 − 66 − 4 = 10 GB to spare: 32,768 tokens of working memory, 20 chats of 1,600 tokens against a peak of 6. It went live on one card at 18:00, at $2,913 a month. Its numbers score predicts about one wrong ticket in a night of 22, against 0.8 under 16 bits, and the morning check still catches them. Obiageli corrected Thursday's three before invoicing and wrote to the two customers who had signed; ticket 502 had gone out that night at £4,370.00, worked out by hand.
options.senior: Squeezing a model loses detail unevenly, so a sign-off must score every smaller copy on every task set the model does, side by side with the full model: run, count, compare, set by set. Here FP8 kept both sets (188 and 153) and fits one card for $2,913 a month; the 4-bit copy kept the English and lost 18 tickets in 160. The next step is to stop asking a model to work out sums at all: let code multiply volume by price and the model copy the total.

options.text: Add 200 more English questions to the sign-off set, then sign off again.
options.verdict: The same blind spot, twice as big
options.part2: Eyvind wrote 200 more English procedure questions on Friday morning. By 15:00 the 400-question set had scored 376 for the 16-bit model and 372 for the 4-bit copy: 1% again, no loss, signed. The 4-bit copy stayed live, and the numbers set was never run. Its tickets kept going wrong about 3 times in a night of 22, as on Thursday. Obiageli's morning check corrected them before invoicing, but every night two or three customers signed a wrong price on site, and Obiageli wrote to each. The bill stayed $2,913 a month.
options.senior: More questions of the same kind measure the same skill more precisely. The English answers were never where the squeeze hurt; the sums were. A sign-off must cover every kind of task the model does, including the ones a small rounding error breaks.

options.text: Go back to the full 16-bit model on two cards, as it ran until 18:00.
options.verdict: Right again, at twice the bill
options.part2: At 16:00 on Friday Eyvind rented the second card again and put the 16-bit model back on two. Tickets were as right as before Thursday: 154 of 160, about 0.8 wrong in a night of 22, and the morning check caught them. Obiageli corrected Thursday's three before invoicing and wrote to the two customers who had signed. The bill went back to $5,825 a month, $2,912 more than one card. Nobody scored an FP8 or INT8 copy, so the next time someone wants the bill halved, the plant starts from the same English-only sign-off.
options.senior: Honest and safe: the full model scored 188 and 154. But it pays $2,912 a month to avoid a measurement. Scoring the smaller copies on every set would have found one that keeps both scores on one card.

options.text: Have the 4-bit model check its own sums on each ticket before printing.
options.part2: From 18:00 on Friday the 4-bit copy worked each total out twice and printed only when the two agreed. A week later, on Friday 25 September, Obiageli asked Eyvind to run the numbers set with the check on: 139 of 160. On 21 of its 24 wrong totals the second try had agreed with the first, because the same squeezed weights did the same sum twice. A night of 22 still brought about 2.9 wrong tickets, and some were signed on site before the morning check found them; Obiageli corrected each one before invoicing and wrote to the customers. The bill stayed $2,913 a month.
options.senior: A model checking its own work repeats its own blind spot: the same rounded weights make the same slip twice. A check helps only when it is independent, such as code that multiplies volume by price. And it still leaves the squeeze unmeasured on everything else the model does.

sim.title: Score the squeezed copies on every set
sim.lede: You're Aslaug at 17:30 on Thursday 17 September, half an hour before the switch. No real model runs here: every figure is worked out from given numbers. Given: Llama 3.1 70B, 70.6 billion weights; in 16-bit about 132 GB, in FP8 about 66 GB, in 4-bit about 33 GB plus about 1 GB of scales. Each chat token keeps 2 × 80 layers × 8 lists × 128 numbers × 2 bytes = 320 KB of working memory; a chat is counted at 1,600 tokens. One NVIDIA H100 holds 80 GB, keeps 4 GB of working space and moves 3.35 TB a second; $3.99 a card hour, 730 hours a month. The plant's own scores, as the week will measure them: English set (200 questions) 16-bit 188, FP8 188, 4-bit 186; numbers set (160 past tickets) 154, 153 and 136. A copy passes a set when it loses no more than 1% of it against 16-bit. Thursday's 22 tickets, three wrong: 484, 493 and 502.
sim.tryThis: Try this: the opening view is Eyvind's sign-off: 4-bit, English only, 186 against 188, pass, numbers not run. Play the night: ticket 502 prints £437.00 against £4,370.00 by hand, 3 of 22 wrong. Now score English and numbers: 136 of 160, 18 more wrong, 3.3 wrong tickets in 22. Try 16-bit on one card, then two: 40 chats, $5,825 a month. Try FP8 on one card: 10 GB, 32,768 tokens, 20 chats against a peak of 6, 188 and 153. Then set the peak to 24 and see who waits. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the cabin was haunted. At 18:00 the assistant became a smaller copy of itself, each weight rounded to 4 bits, and the rounding blurred it unevenly: English answers lost 2 of 200, ticket totals lost 18 of 160. The figures it copied stayed right; the sums it worked out went wrong. The sign-off measured the one skill the squeeze spared.

steps.title: Squeezing: fewer bits a weight.
steps.text: Storing each weight in fewer bits is called quantization. For the 4-bit copy, first the weights are split into groups of 128. Second, each group gets a scale sized to its largest weight. Third, each weight is rounded to the nearest of 16 marks on that scale, where 16 bits allowed 65,536 values. Fourth, when the model runs, each mark is multiplied back by its scale. In FP16 the 70.6 billion weights take 141 billion bytes, about 132 GB; in FP8 or INT8, one byte each, about 66 GB; in INT4 about 33 GB plus 1 GB of scales. Floating point keeps a movable point, so tiny and large weights keep detail more evenly; integers lean on the scale. AWQ first finds the few weights that matter most and protects them before rounding. Fewer bytes also mean faster writing, since every token reads each weight once (a10e01's memory road): at 3.35 TB/s, FP8 on one card at best about 47 tokens a second, the 4-bit copy about 92. What can go wrong: every rounded weight is a little off, and the errors add up through 80 layers.

steps.title: The loss is uneven, and sums go first.
steps.text: An English answer survives a little blur: many wordings are right, and a slightly different word is still right. A ticket total does not: 38 × £115 has one right answer, and one dropped digit makes £437.00. So the same copy lost 2 of 200 English answers and 18 of 160 tickets, 11%, close to Thursday's 3 of 22. On every wrong ticket the volume, mix and price, copied from the order, were right; only the total, worked out by the model, was wrong. Figures a model copies are safer than figures it works out. Marchisio and colleagues found challenging tasks like mathematical reasoning degrade fastest. What can go wrong: a task set that holds only the skill the squeeze spares.

steps.title: Signing off: run, count, compare, on every set.
steps.text: First, list every kind of task the model does: here, procedure answers in English and ticket figures. Second, keep a task set for each, with right answers agreed in advance, like a5e01's golden set and a8e06's old-skills set. Third, run every set on the full model and on each smaller copy. Fourth, count right answers and compare set by set, against a pass bar agreed before scoring, here no more than 1% lost on any set. The plant had the numbers set since April and never put it in the sign-off. What can go wrong: one average over all sets, or one set, hides the set that fell.

steps.title: Tonight's answer: FP8 on one card.
steps.text: Scored on both sets, FP8 got 188 of 200 and 153 of 160: one ticket in 160 lost, within 1%. Kurtic and colleagues report FP8 effectively lossless across all model scales on their tests. Memory: 80 − 66 − 4 = 10 GB left for chats; at 320 KB a token that is 32,768 tokens, 20 chats of 1,600, against a night peak of 6. Cost: one card, $2,913 a month, the same as the 4-bit copy and $2,912 less than 16-bit on two. Its numbers score predicts about one wrong ticket in 22, close to the old 0.8. What can go wrong: a peak that grows past 20 chats, which the cold case meets.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fall short, and where sums belong.
steps.text: 200 more English questions measure the same skill more finely: 376 against 372 of 400 passes, and tickets still go wrong about 3 times in 22. A self-check runs the same squeezed weights twice and agreed with itself on 21 of its 24 wrong totals: 139 of 160. Going back to 16-bit on two cards is right (154) but costs $2,912 a month more. A 4-bit copy of a larger model, such as Llama 3.1 405B, would still be far bigger than one card's 80 GB at half a byte a weight, and would be squeezed the same way. The lasting fix is to take sums away from the model: code multiplies volume by price, and the model only copies the total. Then score every set again. What can go wrong: moving sums into code changes what the numbers set measures, so it must be rebuilt.

diagram.aria: The same model stored three ways, scored on both sets. Left column: 16-bit, FP16, about 132 GB, two cards, $5,825 a month; scores English 188 of 200, numbers 154 of 160. Middle column: FP8, about 66 GB, one card, $2,913, room for 20 chats; scores English 188, numbers 153. Right column: 4-bit, INT4, about 34 GB with scales, one card, $2,913; scores English 186, numbers 136.

notes.text: Same 70.6 billion weights, three sizes, both sets scored

explain.caption: Read each column top to bottom: how the weights are stored, what that costs, then the scores on both sets. Only the numbers set tells the copies apart: FP8 loses one ticket in 160 and fits one card; the 4-bit copy loses 18.

fix.title: The fix: score every smaller copy on every task set, then switch to the smallest that passes them all
fix.text: Before any change to how the model is stored, run every task set the model's work needs, here the English set and the numbers set, on the full model and on each smaller copy: run, count, compare, set by set, against a bar agreed before scoring (no more than 1% lost on any set). Tonight that picks FP8 on one card: 188 and 153, 10 GB left for 20 chats against a peak of 6, $2,913 a month. Keep Obiageli's morning check. Then take the sums away from the model: let code multiply volume by price and hand the model the total to copy, rebuild the numbers set for that, and score again.

limits: A set of 160 tickets cannot tell 153 from 154 apart with any confidence; one ticket is noise. The sets catch big losses like 18 in 160, not small ones, so keep the morning check.

A set measures only the tasks it holds. When the assistant takes on a new kind of task, such as totals across the night's order summary, that task needs its own set before any copy is trusted with it.
The scores, the 6-chat peak and the prices are the plant's own given data. Another model, card or task mix needs its own sets; vLLM's FP8 page lists the cards it supports for this, Hopper among them.
explain.seniorTake: Quantization stores the same model smaller: 16 bits a weight in FP16, 8 in FP8 or INT8, 4 in INT4. Fewer bytes a weight means fewer cards, more room for chats and faster writing, and the price is detail, lost unevenly. Tasks with many right answers, like English prose, barely notice; tasks with one exact answer, like a ticket total, notice first. So the measurement is the whole job: score every smaller copy on every kind of task the model does, side by side with the full model, set by set, against a bar agreed in advance, and pick the smallest copy that passes all of them. Here that was FP8 on one card: the same bill as the 4-bit copy, one ticket in 160 lost instead of 18. And where a figure can be worked out by code, let code do it; a model that copies a figure is safer than one that calculates it.

realWorld.title: GPTQ: 3 or 4 bits on their measures
realWorld.text: Frantar and colleagues' GPTQ paper (ICLR 2023) reports reducing the bitwidth down to 3 or 4 bits per weight, with negligible accuracy degradation relative to the uncompressed baseline, on the measures the paper uses. Those measures are the paper's; a plant's ticket totals are its own, and need their own set.

realWorld.title: AWQ: protect the weights that matter
realWorld.text: Lin and colleagues' AWQ paper (MLSys 2024) says that Protecting only 1% salient weights can greatly reduce quantization error: find the few weights that matter most and keep them sharp before rounding the rest.

realWorld.title: AWQ: 4 bits, and 3
realWorld.text: The abstract names no bit width; the paper's settings section does: We focus on INT4/INT3 quantization since they are able to mostly preserve the LLMs’ performance. Eyvind's copy used the method at 4 bits.

realWorld.title: Maths degrades fastest, and metrics miss it
realWorld.text: Marchisio and colleagues, studying quantized multilingual models, found challenging tasks like mathematical reasoning degrade fastest, and that human evaluators found damage which automatic metrics severely underestimate. Eskmere's English set was the plant's version of a metric that missed it.

realWorld.title: FP8: lossless on their tests
realWorld.text: Kurtic and colleagues ran a large study of quantized Llama 3.1 models and report that FP8 (W8A8-FP) is effectively lossless across all model scales. That is why FP8 was worth scoring first; the plant still checked it on its own sets.

realWorld.title: vLLM: the copies an engine can serve
realWorld.text: vLLM's documentation home page lists Quantization: FP8, MXFP8/MXFP4, NVFP4, INT8, INT4, GPTQ/AWQ among its features, so every copy in this case can be served by the same free engine.

realWorld.title: vLLM: FP8 on the H100
realWorld.text: vLLM's FP8 W8A8 page describes a 2x reduction in model memory requirements with minimal impact on accuracy, and says Ada Lovelace, Hopper, and Blackwell GPUs are supported for W8A8. The H100 is a Hopper card.

realWorld.title: The H100: 80 GB, 3.35 TB/s
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's H100 page lists the H100 SXM with 80GB of GPU memory and 3.35TB/s of memory bandwidth: room for the FP8 copy and its chats on one card, not for the 16-bit model.

realWorld.title: An hour of the card
realWorld.text: Lambda's pricing page, read on 16 October 2026, lists the NVIDIA H100 SXM with 80 GB in four rows from $3.99 to $4.29 per GPU per hour. The story's $3.99 is close to that dollar list price; prices change, and the arithmetic is the lesson.

asked: What do you lose when you quantize a model, and how do you measure it?
FP8 or INT4 for a 70B model on one GPU?
interview.answer: Quantizing stores each weight in fewer bits: rounded to a few marks on a scale kept for each small group, then multiplied back when the model runs. You gain memory and speed: Llama 3.1 70B is about 132 GB in 16 bits, about 66 in FP8 and about 34 in INT4 with scales, so it fits one 80 GB card instead of two, and each token reads fewer bytes. You lose detail, unevenly. Tasks with many acceptable answers, like prose, barely move; tasks with one exact answer, like arithmetic, degrade first; one study of quantized models found mathematical reasoning degrades fastest. So you measure by scoring each squeezed copy side by side with the full model on every task set the system really does, set by set, against a bar agreed beforehand, not on one benchmark or one average. I once saw a 4-bit copy pass a 200-question English sign-off at 186 against 188 and then get 18 more of 160 ticket totals wrong. For a 70B model on one H100 I would score FP8 first: about 66 GB, which leaves about 10 GB for working memory after 4 GB of working space, and FP8 is usually close to lossless. INT4 leaves far more room and roughly doubles the writing speed, but only if it passes every set; where totals matter, I would also move the arithmetic into code.

terms.def: A works that mixes concrete to order and sends it out in drum trucks that keep it turning on the road. Eskmere Concrete runs one in England.
Placing concrete at night, when roads are empty and a site can work without traffic. The plant supplies them from 18:00.
The person who runs the plant's mixing through a shift and signs out each load. Aslaug is Eskmere's on nights.
The plant's own computer that weighs cement, sand, stone and water for each load from its stored recipes. It never asks the assistant, so only paperwork went wrong.
The paper that goes with an order to site: mix, volume, price per cubic metre and total. The customer signs it on arrival. 22 printed from 18:00 to 23:40.
The assistant's list of the night's orders, written for the office from each order's details.
A concrete strength class: the two figures are its strength tested on cylinders and on cubes. Ticket 502's 38 m³ were C32/40.
A cube one metre each way, written m³. Concrete is sold by it: ticket 502 was 38 m³ at £115 each, £4,370.00.
A program that writes text one small piece at a time, having learned from huge amounts of text (a1e01).
A small piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads and writes (a1e03). A chat here is counted at 1,600.
One conversation between a crew member and the assistant. At most 6 were open at once on a night; the cold case's winter peak is 24.
Meta's open-weights language model with 70.6 billion weights, 80 layers and 8 key-value lists per layer. In 16 bits its weights are 141 billion bytes, about 132 GB.
The learned numbers a model is made of (a1e02). Each one is stored in some number of bits: 16, 8 or 4 here.
A bit is one 0 or 1; a byte is 8 bits. A weight in 16 bits takes 2 bytes, in 8 bits one, in 4 bits half a byte.
Gigabyte. The card's meter counts 1 GB as 1,024 MB, so 141 billion bytes shows as about 132 GB; memory speeds use the maker's 1,000.
Short for graphics card: a board with a GPU, a graphics processing unit, and its own memory (a10e01). The plant rents NVIDIA H100s by the hour.
A graphics card with 80 GB of memory and 3.35 TB/s of memory speed. Each keeps 4 GB as working space here; $3.99 a card hour in the story.
Room each card keeps for sums in progress while the model runs, apart from weights and chats: 4 GB a card here.
The keys and values the model keeps for every token of a chat (a10e03): 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 320 KB a token for Llama 3.1 70B.
This season's word for the link from a card's memory to its adders (a10e01). Every token reads each weight along it once, so fewer bytes mean faster writing.
A fixed list of one kind of job with right answers agreed in advance, used to score every version of the model. Eskmere has two: English and numbers.
A fixed list of real inputs with the right answers agreed in advance, kept to score every version of a system (a5e01).
A set of things a model could already do, kept to check a change has not lost them (a8e06). The numbers set could have played that part.
The task set a change must pass before it goes live. Eskmere's has always been the English set: 200 procedure questions.
200 questions about the plant's procedures with agreed answers. 16-bit 188, FP8 188, 4-bit 186.
160 past tickets with checked figures, built by the office in April. 16-bit 154, FP8 153, 4-bit 136. Never in the sign-off.
Approving a change for live use: run the set on each copy, count right answers, compare against a pass bar agreed in advance.
The most a copy may lose against the full model on a set and still pass, agreed before scoring (a5e01). Here 1%: 2 of 200, 1 of 160.
The same model with each weight stored in fewer bits. It knows the same things, a little blurred, like a map redrawn at a smaller scale.
This case's plain word for quantization: split the weights into groups, give each group a scale, round each weight to the nearest mark.
A number kept for each group of 128 weights, sized to its largest, so rounded marks can be multiplied back to size. About 1 GB of them here.
Storing a model's weights in fewer bits than it was trained with, by rounding each to a nearby mark. It saves memory and time and costs detail.
A way to store a number as a few digits plus a point that can move, so tiny and large values both keep detail.
Short for 16-bit floating point: each weight in 2 bytes. Eskmere ran Llama 3.1 70B this way from March: about 132 GB, two cards.
Short for 8-bit floating point: each weight in one byte, about 66 GB for Llama 3.1 70B. It scored 188 and 153 here.
Short for 8-bit integers: each weight a whole number from -128 to 127, with a scale for each group. About the same size as FP8.
Short for 4-bit integers: each weight one of 16 whole-number marks, with a scale per group. About 33 GB plus 1 GB of scales here.
Activation-aware weight quantization: a method that protects the most important weights before rounding the rest. Eyvind's 4-bit copy was made with it.
Another method for squeezing a finished model's weights to 3 or 4 bits; its paper reports negligible accuracy loss on the measures it uses.
Here, figures the model works out rather than copies, such as a ticket's total: volume times price. They went wrong first.
The same model working a figure out a second time and comparing. With the same squeezed weights it repeated 21 of its 24 wrong totals.
The office's daily routine: compare every ticket with its order, then correct any wrong figure before the invoice goes out.
The conditions a seller and buyer agree for each sale, including price. Whether a signed wrong ticket binds anyone depends on them; not legal advice.
A free, widely used serving engine for language models. It can serve FP8, INT8 and INT4 copies, including GPTQ and AWQ ones.
NVIDIA's name for the chip family the H100 belongs to. vLLM's FP8 page lists it among the cards supported for FP8.
The international standard for information security management. Its Annex A control 8.32 covers change management.
The international standard for quality management. Clause 8.5.6 covers control of changes to production or service.
A US auditor's report on a service's controls against the AICPA's trust services criteria. CC8.1 covers change management; PI1 processing integrity.
The SOC 2 category asking that a system's processing be complete, valid, accurate, timely and authorised. A wrong price on a ticket is a failure of it.
The international standard for an AI management system. Its Annex A control A.6.2.4 covers verifying and validating an AI system.
The course's hands-on builds. The Nightwatch copilot's X6 reuses this case: score the self-hosted model's squeezed copy on every set.

atWork: Look for a model swapped for a smaller copy, signed off on one task set. It is a common pattern: a team squeezes a model to save a card, scores it on the questions it always uses, sees a 1% gap, and ships; the first sign of trouble is a figure the model worked out, wrong, in otherwise perfect text. Ask four things. What kinds of task does the model really do, and is there a set with agreed answers for each, including anything it calculates? Were the full model and every smaller copy scored side by side on all of them, against a bar agreed before scoring? Which figures does the model copy and which does it work out, and could code work them out instead? And what still catches a wrong figure after release? Build Night: the Nightwatch copilot's X6 reuses this case: when you compare a small self-hosted model with an API model, score its squeezed copy on every set; a later build project will ask you to measure this. Standards-readiness note, stated conditionally and not legal advice: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, an auditor checking Annex A 8.32 (change management, as summarised by a third-party guide) would look for test results on every task set before a model change goes live; one checking ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.5.6 (control of changes, as summarised by a certification body) would look for the same review before the switch. If you report against SOC 2, an auditor checking CC8.1 (change management) would look for tested, approved changes, and one checking processing integrity (PI1) would look at how wrong prices are prevented and corrected. If you work to ISO/IEC 42001:2023, control A.6.2.4 (AI system verification and validation, as summarised by a third-party guide) is likely to expect a model change to be tested before release. None of these notes is legal advice.

recall.prompt: A builders' merchant serves Llama 3.1 70B in 16 bits on two cards to write customer quotes: item lines, quantities, unit prices and totals. IT wants a 4-bit copy on one card to halve the bill. Its sign-off: 300 questions about products, 16-bit 282, 4-bit 279, within 1%. What do you ask for before it goes live?

keyIdeas.idea: Squeezing loses detail unevenly, and figures the model works out, like totals, usually suffer first, so a product-question set can pass while totals go wrong
Score the copy side by side with the full model on every kind of task it does, including a set of past quotes with checked totals
Score an 8-bit copy (FP8) too and choose the smallest copy that passes every set

recall.model: Before it goes live I want it scored on every task the assistant does, not one set. Squeezing to 4 bits loses detail unevenly: figures the model works out, like a quote's total, usually suffer first, while answers about products barely move, so 279 against 282 says nothing about the totals. Build a set of past quotes with checked totals and run it side by side on the 16-bit model and the 4-bit copy: run, count, compare, against a bar agreed before scoring. Score an FP8 copy as well, which is about half the 16-bit size and usually close to lossless, and pick the smallest copy that passes every set. And where code can calculate a total, let it, so the model only copies it.

recall.prompt: Llama 3.1 70B has 70.6 billion weights. About how much memory do they take stored in FP8, on a meter that counts 1 GB as 1,024 MB?
recall.why: FP8 stores each weight in one byte: 70.6 billion bytes, which the meter shows as about 66 GB. About 132 GB is 16 bits (2 bytes a weight); about 33 GB is 4 bits, before the scales.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: what do you lose when you quantize a model, and how do you measure it?

keyIdeas.idea: Rounding each weight to fewer bits loses detail, unevenly: tasks with one exact answer, like arithmetic, degrade first
Measure by scoring the squeezed copy side by side with the full model on every task set, against a bar agreed in advance
What you gain: fewer bytes per weight, so fewer cards, more room and faster writing; pick the smallest copy that passes

recall.model: You lose detail. Quantizing rounds each weight to a few marks on a scale kept for each small group, so every weight is a little off, and the loss is uneven: tasks with many acceptable answers, like prose, barely move, while tasks with one exact answer, like arithmetic, degrade first. You gain fewer bytes per weight: a 70B model goes from about 132 GB in 16 bits to about 66 in FP8 and about 34 in INT4, so it needs fewer cards, leaves more room for working memory and gives faster writing. To measure it, score the squeezed copy side by side with the full model on every task set the system really does, set by set, against a bar agreed in advance, and pick the smallest copy that passes every set.

recall.prompt: FP8 Llama 3.1 70B (about 66 GB) runs on one 80 GB card that keeps 4 GB of working space. Each token keeps 320 KB of working memory. How many chats of 1,600 tokens fit?
recall.why: 80 − 66 − 4 = 10 GB for chats. 10 GB is 10,485,760 KB; ÷ 320 KB = 32,768 tokens; ÷ 1,600 = 20 chats. 40 is 16-bit on two cards (20 GB); 10 is the GB, not the chats.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. FP8 has run on one card since Friday 18 September; both sets are now run on every change, and tickets slip about as often as they did before that Thursday. From Monday 7 December a second night crew started on winter pours, and on Thursday 10 December the assistant's peak reached 24 chats at once, with some of the crew waiting for a free chat. Eyvind's note: go back to the 4-bit copy, it has room for 86 chats on one card, and the bill stays the same.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. How many chats does FP8 on one card hold, what would Eyvind's change cost the plant, and what would you do instead?

keyIdeas.idea: FP8 on one card has 10 GB for chats: 32,768 tokens, 20 chats of 1,600, so 4 of the 24 wait
The 4-bit copy fits 86 but scored 136 of 160 on the numbers set: about 3 wrong tickets a night, September again
Add room without losing the sums: a second card for FP8 (176 chats, $5,825 a month), or move totals into code and re-score the 4-bit copy on every set first

coldCase.model: Not the 4-bit copy. FP8 on one card leaves 80 − 66 − 4 = 10 GB for chats: 32,768 tokens at 320 KB, 20 chats of 1,600, so at a peak of 24, 4 wait. The 4-bit copy has room for 86, but it scored 136 of 160 on the numbers set, 18 more wrong than 16-bit: about 3 wrong tickets in a night of 22, September again, signed on site. Instead, rent a second card for the FP8 copy: 176 chats, $5,825 a month, the scores unchanged. Or move each ticket's total into code, so the model copies a sum instead of working it out, rebuild the numbers set for that, and re-score the 4-bit copy on every set before any switch.
